abstract: Highlights • LTBP1 and MAGP1 are expressed in corneal stroma during development and in mature corneas. • LTBP1 and MAGP1 accumulate in corneal stroma matrix with development. • Latent TGF β accumulates in the stroma with development. • LTBP1 regulates transformation of fibroblasts to myofibroblasts in vitro .
methods:
Materials and methods
Animals
.
Wild-type, C57BL/6, mice were used for studies evaluating the expression of LTBP1 and MAGP1 in stromal development. The dissected whole corneas from adult mice (60 days old) were examined. All experiments conformed to the use of Laboratory Animals and ARVO statement for the Use of Animals in Ophthalmic and Vision Research and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of South Florida College of Medicine. All mice were handled in accordance with NIH's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
body:
Introduction
The extracellular matrix is a complex structure that regulates tissue function, as well as directs resident cell function and differentiation.[
1
,
2
] The unique composition of the extracellular matrix is specific to each tissue and provides chemical and physical cues to resident cells.[
[2]
,
[3]
,
[4]
,
[5]
] The corneal matrix consists mostly of collagen fibrils and some proteoglycans.[
[5]
,
[6]
,
[7]
,
[8]
,
[9]
,
[10]
,
[11]
] Old and recent electron microscopy studies have suggested the presence of elastic fibers too in minimal quantities.[
[12]
,
[13]
,
[14]
] Collagen molecules and fibrils −main components of the corneal stroma- undergo changes with aging and bestow the stroma most of its unique mechanical properties including stiffness.[
[15]
,
[16]
,
[17]
] Studies using small-angle and wide-angle x-ray scattering, techniques not influenced by fixation, have demonstrated that collagen fibril diameter and inter-collagen molecule space (intermolecular Bragg spacing) increase with age.[
15
,
18
] Collagen fibrils are organized into lamellae and run parallel to the corneal surface. Lamellar branching occurs only in the anterior cornea of mammals but not in the posterior stroma where collagen lamellae run parallel to each other.[
19
,
20
].
Elastic fibers confer tissues with flexibility and pliability, properties that decline with age and are essential for expandable tissues like aorta, lungs and skin.[
[21]
,
[22]
,
[23]
,
[24]
,
[25]
,
[26]
] The major constituents of the elastic fibers are elastin (fiber core component), fibrillin microfibrils (scaffold for elastic fiber formation), and associated proteins essential for elastic fiber function including LTBP1 and MAGP1. However, some tissues can express LTBP1 and MAGP1 without containing elastic fibers, i.e., lens zonules. The expression of fibrillin in the cornea has been documented in the entire stroma of bovine and mouse corneas.[
12
,
27
,
28
] Fibrillin expression in adult human stroma has been reported in the far peripheral cornea close to Descemet’s membrane (DM) −using immunofluorescence microscopy- and in the central stroma in patient with bullous keratopathy using immunogold electron microscopy.[
27
,
29
] During human corneal development fibrillin expression is detected at early gestation but not in corneas of 3 years old toddlers where fibrillin expression is localized to DM only.[
30
].
The transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) signaling system regulates various cell functions, including cell proliferation, differentiation, and death.[
[31]
,
[32]
,
[33]
,
[34]
] In the cornea, TGF-β signaling system is known to be a major modulator of cell function and fibrosis during wound healing.[
[35]
,
[36]
,
[37]
] Cells secrete an inactive TGF-β protein into the extracellular matrix. Inside the endoplasmic reticulum, TGF-β Latency Associated Peptide (LAP) dimers form two disulfide bonds to the chaperone proteins LTBP1 and LTBP3.[
38
] Once secreted into the extracellular space, TGF-β storage and activation are regulated by the extracellular matrix where LTBP1 binds fibronectin and fibrillin.[
[38]
,
[39]
,
[40]
] LTBP1 plays a critical role in modulating the function of TGF-β by controlling its storage and mechanical release from the extracellular matrix.[
39
,
[41]
,
[42]
,
[43]
,
[44]
].
To our knowledge, corneal expression of LTBP1 and MAGP1, both regulators of TGF-β activation and elastic fiber associated proteins have not been comprehensively studied in the mechanically stiff collagen rich stroma. This study aims to investigate the expression of LTBP1 and MAGP1 in stromal development and evaluate the regulation of stromal TGF-β latency and activation in the cornea by LTBP1. Understanding the regulation of TGF-β latency and activation in the stroma has significant translational implications for wound healing and corneal fibrosis.
Results
Spatial LTBP1 and MAGP1 expression in the mouse stroma
.
The patterns of spatial expression of LTBP1 in adult murine corneas (90 days old mice) using immuno–fluorescence microscopy revealed LTBP1 expression throughout the entire stroma
(
Fig. 1
)
. A fibrillar pattern of staining was noted with predominance of a vertical orientation near DM that was densest towards the membrane
(
Fig. 1A,C
)
. There was also a mixed horizontal and vertical orientation in the remaining stroma. A posterior to anterior expression gradient was noticeable with decreased expression in the anterior stroma. Increased staining of LTBP1 was seen in the region of trabecular meshwork and next to DM
(
Fig. 1B
)
. MAGP1 expression was present throughout the cornea in a spatial pattern identical to the denser posterior to anterior expression gradient of LTPB1
(
Fig. 2
)
. The pattern of expression was different from collagen fibrils and collagen lamella that run a horizontal pattern parallel to the corneal surface as seen in second harmonic generation microscopy
(
Fig. 2C
)
and as it has been described in the literature.[
19
,
20
] Controls using isotypic control IgG as primary antibody showed no staining −data not shown-.

Spatial LTBP1 and MAGP1 expression in porcine and human stroma
Human and porcine stromas showed significant LTBP1 expression in a pattern like that found in mouse corneas. In porcine tissue, dense expression closest to DM was evident
(
Fig. 3
)
. A significantly higher expression was noted in the posterior stroma as it approached DM and that decreased in intensity towards the central and anterior stroma.

Human tissue had a similar pattern to mouse and porcine tissue but lacked the characteristic lattice-like staining noted in the other two species. Denser staining was observed in the pre-DM region
(

)
. Minimal or no LTBP1 staining was noted in human and porcine sclera.

Temporal LTBP1 and MAGP1 expression during murine corneal development and homeostasis
To assess the role of LTBP1 in corneal development, temporal expression was examined at different stages of life: immature (days 1–30), maturing (days 31–89) and adult (day 90 and older).
Ltbp1
expression was highest and peaked at an early postnatal age (4 days of age) then decreased with maturation. A significant difference was seen between 4 and 30 days of age, p = 0.0002,
t
-test.
Ltbp1
was still expressed at 140 days of age. When protein expression was evaluated, LTBP1 was present from an early age (4 days) and then progressively more LTBP1 protein was deposited and accumulated in the matrix, peaking at around 90 days of age. A statistical significant difference was present between 10 and 150 days of age, p = 0.02,
t
-test.
(
Fig. 5
)
.
Mfap2
RNA expression followed LTBP1 pattern with higher synthesis during stromal development. A significant difference was noted between 4 and 30 days of age, p = 0.004,
t
-test.
(
Fig. 5D
)
. This pattern in LTBP1 and MAGP1 expression suggests a role of these matrix components in corneal development and maturation.

The area under the curve (AUC) of the protein of interest was divided by the AUC of the total protein to determine the normalized relative protein levels. The AUC was calculated by the WES Compass for SW software. Normalization with total protein uses a chemiluminescent method with biotin labeling of all proteins, detected via streptavidin-HRP and luminol/peroxide substrate, ensuring a signal proportional to total protein concentration. Welch’s
t
-test was used for statistical analyses where bars show mean and SEM.
Total TGF-β1 content increases with stromal maturation
Our data show that
Ltbp1
and
Mfap2
synthesis is high during stromal development and decreases with maturation. However, LTBP1 progressively accumulates in the stroma with maturation and high protein expression is maintained in the stroma and found after 90 days of age. To explore if LTBP1 accumulation increases total TGF-β content in the cornea, a very sensitive and functional assay based on the upregulation of PAI-1 by TGF-β was employed.[
45
] We assessed the amount of total TGF-β in stroma at two different ages (30 and 90 days old). We activated total TGF-β stored in stroma by heating exactly similar quantities of stromal extracts from WT corneas for 10 min at 80 °C. Total TGF-β was then measured using transformed mink lung reporter cells, which synthesize luciferase as a function of active TGF-β. To make sure that PAI-1 promoter was activated by TGF-β and no other growth factors, we tested luciferase synthesis after the use of SB-431542. We found that total TGF-β deposits were significantly higher in the older WT matrix (
t
-test, p = 0.04)
(
Fig. 6A
)
. These findings suggest that latent TGF-β reserves are deposited in the stroma with maturation and are maintained in stroma as it ages.

LTBP1 regulates functional activation of latent TGF β
in vitro
by corneal derived myofibroblasts
Once we demonstrated that LTBP1 as well as latent TGF β in the corneal stroma increase with age, we wanted to explore if LTBP1 regulated the activation of latent TGF β by corneal cells during tissue repair. Myofibroblasts are essential during wound healing and activate latent TGF β by mechanically pulling on LTBP1
in vitro
.[
46
] We have shown that corneal derived myofibroblasts activate latent TGF β −deposited on the culture dish- better than fibroblasts.[
47
] To understand the regulation of LTBP1 in the activation of latent TGF β by myofibroblasts, we cultured two groups of corneal derived fibroblasts until confluency, with and without
Ltbp1
silencing. Each group was then stimulated to become myofibroblasts by adding 5 ng/ml human recombinant TGF β1 (Sigma).[
47
] Measurements of TGF β activity was performed by collecting supernatant (medium) from myofibroblasts cultures on serum free medium (DMEM only) for three different periods (1 min, 1 hr. and 3 hrs.). We next stimulated CAGA cells with collected medium to functionally quantify active TGF β released by myofibroblasts from a deposited matrix with and without LTBP1. Myofibroblasts in a
Ltbp1
silenced matrix activated more TGF β than controls in the first 1 h but at 3 h decreased amounts of LTBP1 in the deposited matrix reduced the amount of TGF β that was released to the medium by myofibroblasts
(
Fig. 6B
)
. These findings suggest that lack of LTBP1 in deposited matrix reduces the amount of latent stored TGF β. Decreased LTBP1 in deposited matrix downregulates the amount of active TGF β that can be released by myofibroblasts to the medium. LTBP1 traps and keeps TGF β latent, preventing its activation by myofibroblasts.
LTBP1 regulates myofibroblast conversion from corneal derived fibroblasts
in vitro
After we showed that LTBP1 regulates TGF β latency and activation by corneal derived myofibroblasts, we wanted to further explore the possible roles of silencing
Ltbp1
on the conversion of fibroblasts to α-SMA (smooth muscle actin expressing) myofibroblasts. Corneal derived fibroblasts were allowed to attach and grow to 40–50 % confluency under 10 % serum-containing medium. Cells were then maintained on a medium containing only 1 % FBS and a control group was transfected with a control
shRen 713 −
not affecting LTBP1 synthesis-. In a second group, LTBP1 expression was silenced using
shltbp1
. Protein and mRNA were analyzed after cells were in 1 % FBS for 4–5 days
(
Fig. 7A and C
)
. Immunofluorescence microscopy suggested increased expression of α-SMA in the absence of LTBP1
(Fig. B)
. Quantitatively, a statistically significant higher number of myofibroblasts −defined by expression of α-SMA- was present when
Ltbp1
expression was silenced. This was demonstrated at the transcription (p < 0.0001,
t
-test) and protein level (p < 0.03,
t
-test),
(
Fig. 7A and C
).
To further confirm the role of LTBP1 in regulating myofibroblast conversion, proteomic evaluation of selected proteins, known to be upregulated by myofibroblasts [
48
] was done by comparing cell lysates obtained from myofibroblasts with normal (control
shREN713
) and silenced LTBP1 expression. Increased expression of focal adhesion components, thrombospondin, and α-SMA were present in a matrix deficient in LTBP1
(
Fig. 7D
)
. Together, these findings suggested that LTBP1 deposited in the matrix is a regulator of fibroblast to myofibroblast conversion.

Discussion
The transforming growth factor (TGF)-β cytokine system regulates multiple cell functions in the body.[
37
,
49
] A major regulator of extracellular matrix synthesis and cell function (including myofibroblast differentiation), TGF-β is at the same time significantly modulated by components of the elastic system (LTBP1, MAGPs and fibrillin) present in the extracellular matrix (
Fig. 8
). [
[50]
,
[51]
,
[52]
] In this study, we demonstrate that LTBP1 and MAGP1 are expressed in the corneal stroma and that LTBP1 plays a role in regulating TGF-β latency and activation −potentially modulating fibroblasts and myofibroblasts phenotype-.
Fig. 8
Summary diagram shows the spatial expression of LTBP1 and MAGP1in the mammal cornea. A denser expression is noted in the posterior cornea where it is expressed in a horizontal fashion in proximity to DM. In the central stroma a vertical and horizontal pattern of expression is noted. It is unknown if the spatial expression correlates to function in different areas of the stroma. BL: Bowman layer, S: Stroma, DM: Descemet’s membrane.
Many matrix proteins provide a substrate for presenting growth factors as well as sequestering active and latent cytokines that regulate development and cell function.[
3
,
53
] As the extracellular matrix changes during development and after injury, the availability of matrix-associated growth factors for signaling evolves accordingly. These changes will eventually dictate cell function.[
2
] Until now, the presence of LTBP1 and MAGP1 in the cornea has not been well established or characterized. These proteins are produced and deposited in the stroma during development and their synthesis decelerates with stromal maturation. They not only form a scaffold for matrix formation and matrix biomechanical function but in many tissues −aorta, skin and lungs-, elastic fibrils modulate TGF-β signaling.[
7
,
[21]
,
[22]
,
[23]
,
52
].
Regulation of TGF-β storage, release and bioavailability by different components of the extracellular matrix is currently a subject of intense interest in several fields of biology, including cancer.[
38
,
39
,
42
,
54
] Collagens VI and XII are examples of matrix regulators of TGF-β signaling.[
55
,
56
] We have shown that increased TGF-β activity occurs in the
Col12a1
-/-
cornea.[
56
] Similar findings were recently reported in the skin of mutant mice deficient in
Col12a1
-/-
.[
57
] Another group of matrix components known to regulate stromal function are the proteoglycans. Six proteoglycans are expressed in the stroma: decorin, biglycan, lumican, keratocan, fibromodulin, and osteoglycin. Proteoglycans act as tissue organizers, regulate cell growth, modulate and anchor TGF-β, bind water through their GAG chains to regulate hydration, and regulate collagen fibrillogenesis.[
7
,
10
,
11
,
58
] Decorin, biglycan and fibromodulin bind TGF-β and potentially regulate its effects on cells and tissue repair after injury.[
7
,
59
].
The possible roles of LTBP1 in regulating TGF-β latency during stromal development is an interesting area of investigation. Do keratocytes continuously activate latent TGF-β to maintain tissue integrity during homeostasis? We found through protein blotting that stromal content of LTBP1 increases during cornea development. Our luciferase assay showed higher total TGF-β in old corneas suggesting increased latent TGF-β stromal storage with aging. It could be hypothesized that the main function of LTBP1 is to store latent TGF-β to maintain homeostasis or for use in acute stress (e.g., infections or injuries). More research is needed to validate this idea. Although our experiments show novel data −similar temporal and spatial expression of MAGP1-, we have no data that demonstrate that MAGP1 is functionally regulating TGF-β latency.
Based on the pattern of spatial and temporal expression of MAGP1 and LTBP1, we hypothesize that corneal development and maturation are regulated by the availability of TGF-β. Its latency could be modulated by a balance between a predominantly softer matrix (early in development higher proportional content of LTBP than collagens) and a rigid collagenous matrix (formed later during maturation and aging by continuous matrix deposition of fibrillar collagens and tissue crosslinking). We propose that during development, a softer matrix facilitates the activation of latent TGF-β by keratocytes, increasing matrix synthesis and promoting collagen deposition and upregulating tissue stiffness. Once a certain degree of stromal stiffness is achieved during matrix maturation, keratocytes trapped in a denser and stiffer matrix activate less latent TGF-β from the surrounding stroma, and the rigid collagenous matrix will predominate over the early more elastic matrix. This is functionally manifest as the less pliable aging matrix.
Understanding the regulation of TGF-β latency and activation by the stromal matrix has multiple implications for understanding stromal diseases including ectasias and scarring after injury. Our
in vitro
studies clearly point to two important roles for LTBP1 in the cornea: 1- facilitating TGF-β latency in the matrix; 2- regulating conversion of corneal fibroblasts to myofibroblasts. These two roles that are demonstrable
in vitro
- suggest a critical role for LTBP1 in tissue repair and wound healing. Although multiple matrix components are known to modulate TGF-β latency −fibrillin, decorin, collagens VI, XII, and LTBP3-, our data show that LTBP1 is essential to trap and inactivate TGF-β in the cornea keeping it latent. If LTBP1 is not present, we believe active TGF-β levels will be constantly increased and that would explain the increased expression of α-SMA (higher myofibroblast conversion) seen in the
shLTBP1
group in cultures of fibroblasts without TGF-β supplementation. The mechanisms behind a higher myofibroblast conversion in the absence of LTBP1 remain speculative. If we extrapolate this to a plausible
in vivo
injury model, constantly increased TGF-β levels will hypothetically favor a fibrotic response after injury with increased numbers of myofibroblasts. We are currently working on a transgenic mouse model where we can manipulate LTBP1 expression to validate the findings of this manuscript
in vivo
. Direct
in vivo
functional data will validate our
in vitro
findings and hypotheses.
Our laboratory endeavors are focused on better understanding the role of cellular components and the matrix in corneal wound healing. Future works is needed to establish the roles that LTBP1 plays
in vivo
during tissue repair. The data presented from this study show that the corneal stroma contains latent TGF-β stored in the matrix that most likely regulates tissue development and repair. Our current studies aim to deepen our comprehension of the cellular mechanisms regulated by LTBP1 using transgenic mouse models. A better understanding of how LTBP1 is regulated and the roles it plays during tissue repair has translational potential that could alter the clinical course of corneal scarring.
Materials and methods
Animals
.
Wild-type, C57BL/6, mice were used for studies evaluating the expression of LTBP1 and MAGP1 in stromal development. The dissected whole corneas from adult mice (60 days old) were examined. All experiments conformed to the use of Laboratory Animals and ARVO statement for the Use of Animals in Ophthalmic and Vision Research and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of South Florida College of Medicine. All mice were handled in accordance with NIH's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
Corneal tissue
Human cornea tissue was obtained from the Lions Eye Bank (Tampa, FL) and were harvested from cadaver eyes (adult males over 60 years of age). Removed corneas were immediately stored in Optisol storage medium (Chiron Ophthalmics, Irvine, CA) at 4 °C until use. Corneal tissues were obtained from cadaveric donors. Since no personal identifiable information was available, institutional review board approval was not required. Fresh pig corneas (4 months old) were obtained from local slaughterhouse and arrived at the laboratory within 24 h after euthanasia while maintained at 4 °C.
Isolation and culture of corneal fibroblasts
After euthanasia, the eyes of P60 C57BL/6, mice were immersed in Betadine ophthalmic solution and then incubated in DMEM containing 15 mg/ml dispase II (Roche Applied Science) at 4 °C for 18 h. The entire corneal epithelium sheet loosened by this treatment was removed by vigorous shaking. Under a dissecting microscope, the stroma was separated from sclera at the corneoscleral limbus by pressing down the limbus with a 27-gauge needle.[
60
] Isolated corneal stromas were incubated overnight at 37 °C in DMEM containing 1.25 mg/ml collagenase A (Roche Applied Science) and 25 μg/ml gentamicin. A keratocyte-containing cell suspension was then seeded on plastic dishes in DMEM containing 25 μg/ml gentamicin supplemented with 5 % fetal bovine serum (FBS). When cells reached confluence, the same medium was switched to 1 % FBS and supplemented with 0.1 mM L- ascorbic acid phosphate to enhance collagen synthesis and matrix formation. To study TGF-β mechanical activation, a group of fibroblasts was transformed to myofibroblasts by adding 5 ng/ml of human recombinant TGF-β (Sigma). Myofibroblasts were left on DMEM for 1 min, 1 h and 3 h and medium collected to study the amount of activated TGF-β (by a functional luciferase assay) in the presence or absence of a matrix containing LTBP1.
Immunofluorescence microscopy
Once corneas were harvested, they were embedded in OCT medium and frozen using isopentane.[
61
] Corneal sections −5––7 µm thick- were blocked using 10 % donkey serum (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO). Sections were incubated with rabbit anti-LTBP1 antibody[
46
] (1:100 dilution, generous gift of Dr. Carl-Henrik Heldin, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden) and rabbit anti-MAGP1 antibody[
62
] (1:100 dilution, generous gift of Dr. Robert Mecham, Washington University, St Louis, MO, USA) for 1 h at room temperature. The secondary antibody was Alexa Fluor 568 donkey anti–rabbit IgG (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, Ca) used at 1:200 dilution. DAPI Fluoromount-G® clear mounting solution (Southern Biotech) with DAPI was used as a nuclear marker. Images were captured using a fluorescence microscope (Leica DM5500B). Identical conditions and negative controls were used to facilitate comparisons between samples.
Second harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy
Corneal tissue sections (10–12 μm thick) were imaged using an Olympus MPE-RS microscope using a 25x (0.95NA) (Olympus). Corneal sections 5––7 µm were imaged to investigate stromal structure using SHG microscopy. Second harmonic generation (SHG) signals were created by a titanium:sapphire laser at 960 nm. The SHG forward-scattered signals passing through the corneal sections were collected using a 0.8NA condenser lens with a narrow band-pass filter (465–485 nm). All samples were scanned using a 2-µm z-axis step size.
RNA isolation and quantification of mRNA
Whole corneas were dissected from wild-type mice at ages P4, P10, P30, P90 and P150 and Corneal tissue was incubated with Dispase II to remove the epithelium. The stroma was cut into small pieces as previously described.[
61
] Reverse transcription and quantitative real-time PCR analysis was performed as described before.[
61
] The following primer sequences were used:
Mfap2
: FW: 5′-CACAAGCCTTGCAAACAGTG-3′; RV: 5′-TGCGGACACATATTTCCTTG-3′;
Ltbp1
: FW: 5′-ATGGATTCCAGCTGAACGAC-3′; RV: 5′-ACTCCCCATGAGATCCACAG-3′; β-actin (
Actb
) FW: AGATGACCCAGATCATGTTTGAGA, RV: CACAGCCTGGATGGCTACGT. Each sample was run in duplicate PCR reaction, statistical analysis was performed on 3–6 corneas of different mice at each time point.
Quantitation of protein expression
Corneas from wild-type mice, P4, P10, P14, P30, P90, and P150 were cut into small pieces so that 2 to 5 corneas were pooled for protein extraction using radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) lysis buffer. Protein concentration was determined through a bicinchoninic acid assay (BCA, Thermo Scientific Pierce). LTBP1 expression was analyzed using WES (ProteinSimple, San Jose, California) simple western system following manufacturer instructions. 12–230 kDa separation module, anti-rabbit detection module, and total protein detection module were applied. Briefly, samples diluted with 0.1X sample buffer (ProteinSimple, San Jose, California) at concentration of 0.5 μg/μl were loaded and hybridized with anti-LTBP1 antibody (1:1000 dilution).[
63
] Total protein was used as a loading control.
Mass Spectrometry and proteomics analysis
To analyze if LTBP1 regulates the conversion of fibroblasts to myofibroblasts and the expression of different proteins in a myofibroblast matrix, control (
shRen 713

Proteomic analysis
Protein extracted from corneal myofibroblasts was lysed in 50 mmol/L triethylammonium bicarbonate buffer, pH 7.55, containing 5 % SDS. To ensure no DNA remained to prevent the trap from clogging, the solution was then sheered thoroughly by probe sonication at 20 % amplitude, 5 s on 5 s off, for 30 s. A S-Trap micro column (Protifi brand) was placed in a 1.7 mL tube to retain flowthrough. The sample mixture was then added into the micro column in 200 µl aliquots, followed by centrifugation of the micro column at 4,000 x g for 1 min. After removal of the flow-through, the process was repeated until the entire sample had passed through the S-Trap. The S-Trap micro column was then capped to limit evaporative loss without forming an airtight seal and incubated in a heat block at 37
ο
C overnight. After digestion, peptides were eluted first with 40 µL of 50 mM TEAB. Peptides from cultured cells were characterized using a Thermo Q-exactive-HF mass spectrometer was equipped with a Thermo nanospray Flex source and protein identification done as previously described.[
64
].

An oligonucleotide-targeting Renilla Luciferase (Ren 713) was used as a control. Plasmid DNA was amplified and purified using a HiSpeed Plasmid Midi kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany) and then transfected along with packaging plasmid using JetPrime (Polyplus transfection, NY, USA) into HEK293T cells to generate lentiviruses. Luciferase assay
Transformed mink lung cells (TMLC) transfected with luciferase cDNA driven by PAI-1 promoter were used.[
45
,
56
] TMLCs were expanded in DMEM supplemented with 10 % FBS (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA). For analysis and quantification of latent TGF-β in murine corneas of different ages, corneal stromas were sectioned into 4 pieces with a blade and heated at 80 °C for 10 min to release latent TGF-β. Equal amounts of protein extract measured with Pierce BCA protein kit assay (Gibco) were added to TMLC for incubation for 16 h under serum-free conditions. For analysis and quantification of active TGF-β, TMLC were seeded and allowed to attach for 4 h and in serum-free DMEM and then 100 μl of medium obtained from stromal tissue or from culture medium was added to the cells. TGF-β signaling was inhibited by the addition of the TGF-β type I receptor/ALK5 inhibitor, SB431542 (Tocris Bioscience, Minneapolis, MN, USA) to 10 μM final concentration as control −data not shown-.[
56
] Luciferase assay was carried out using Promega's Luciferase Assay System (Promega, Madison, WI), and luminance measured with a Synergy HT plate reader (BIO-TEK, Winooski, VT).
Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed with GraphPad Prism version 9.1.2 (San Diego, CA, USA). All data are shown as means ± standard deviation. Statistical significance was evaluated by unpaired two tailed Student
t
-test or Welch’s
t
-test. Statistically significant was identified at three levels: *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01; ***P < 0.005; and ****P < 0.001.
